lesson.title: Spotting a Squared Binomial: The Perfect Square Trinomial
lesson.summary: Squaring a binomial always produces a trinomial with a specific structure, first term squared, last term squared, and a middle term equal to twice their product, that you can learn to recognize on sight.
lesson.body:
When you square a binomial, (a + b)^2 or (a - b)^2, the special products pattern always produces the same kind of trinomial: a^2 + 2ab + b^2, or a^2 - 2ab + b^2 for the subtraction case. Because both outcomes are the result of squaring a binomial, trinomials with this exact structure are called perfect square trinomials. Learning to recognize the pattern lets you go from a trinomial back to its squared binomial form almost instantly.

A trinomial passes the perfect square test when three things line up. First, the leading term must be a perfect square, such as x^2 or 9x^2. Second, the constant term must also be a perfect square, such as 25 or 16. Third, and this is the step students most often skip, the middle term must equal exactly twice the product of the square roots of the first and last terms. If all three conditions hold, the trinomial factors as the square of a binomial, with the sign of the middle term deciding whether it is a sum or a difference being squared.

Take x^2 + 10x + 25. The first term, x^2, has square root x. The last term, 25, has square root 5. Twice their product is 2 times x times 5, which is 10x, and that matches the middle term exactly. So the trinomial is a perfect square, and it factors as (x + 5)^2. Confirm this by expanding: (x + 5)(x + 5) gives x^2 + 5x + 5x + 25, and combining the middle terms, 5x + 5x is 10x, gives back x^2 + 10x + 25.

The pattern holds just as well when the binomial itself has a coefficient. Consider (3x + 2)^2. Squaring gives (3x)^2 + 2 times 3x times 2 + 2^2, which is 9x^2 + 12x + 4. Reading this trinomial back, the first term 9x^2 has square root 3x, the last term 4 has square root 2, and twice their product, 2 times 3x times 2, is 12x, matching the middle term exactly, so the test confirms the trinomial is indeed (3x + 2)^2. A numeric check with x = 1 gives 9 + 12 + 4 = 25 on one side and (3 + 2)^2 = 25 on the other, which agree.

The middle term test matters because not every trinomial with two perfect square terms is a perfect square trinomial. Consider x^2 + 8x + 25: the first and last terms are still perfect squares, but twice the product of their roots is 2 times x times 5, or 10x, which does not match the actual middle term of 8x. This trinomial fails the test and is not the square of a binomial. Running this same three part test in reverse, on a trinomial you are given rather than one you built, is exactly the skill covered later under factoring perfect square trinomials.

It is also worth contrasting this pattern with the difference of squares from the previous section, since both involve two perfect square terms and students sometimes mix them up. A difference of squares, a^2 - b^2, has exactly two terms and no middle term at all. A perfect square trinomial has three terms, and its defining feature is precisely that nonzero middle term equal to twice the product of the square roots. Seeing two squared terms is not enough on its own to tell you which pattern, if either, applies; you have to look at how many terms there are and whether a matching middle term is present.
